facts.claim: Increasing the depth of information shared in a social network profile reduced interpersonal attraction.
facts.quote: Analyses indicated that, while increasing the breadth of information had a positive impact on interpersonal attraction to profile owners, increasing the depth of information reduced attraction.

facts.claim: Increasing the depth of information shared in a social network profile enhanced attributional confidence only when the breadth of information shared was low.
facts.quote: Additionally, there was a significant interaction between breadth and depth of information in predicting attributional confidence; increasing the depth of information shared in an SNS profile enhanced attributional confidence only when the breadth of information shared was low.

facts.claim: Increasing the breadth of information shared in a social network profile increased interpersonal attraction.
facts.quote: Analyses indicated that, higher breadth of information shared in the profile increased interpersonal attraction and that attributional confidence mediated this relationship.

facts.claim: Feelings of being alone were correlated with the frequency of talking to oneself and using the TV for company.
facts.quote: Study 1 ( N = 240) found that ratings of how alone participants felt were correlated with frequency of talking to themselves and using the TV for company.

facts.claim: Loneliness was correlated with talking to oneself and singing to oneself.
facts.quote: Study 2 ( N = 66) was a daily diary study where loneliness was correlated with both Study 1 behaviors and singing to oneself.

research.angle: While sharing more breadth of information on social networks increases attraction, sharing deeper information can actually reduce it.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that social network profile depth can decrease interpersonal attraction and that loneliness is linked to behaviors that trick the brain into feeling socially interactive.
research.caveat: The studies on social network profiles do not measure subjective well-being or the specific impact of high-frequency, low-depth interactions with friends.
